verses.note: These verses define what a prophet is: a mouth for another's words. The relation between Moses and Aaron models the relation between God and his prophets, whose authority lies entirely in speaking what they have been given (2 Peter 1:21).

The prophet's task is to say everything God says, no more and no less. The command anticipates the arrangement in 7:1-2, where Moses speaks all that God commands and Aaron carries it to Pharaoh, and it is the standard Jeremiah is held to (Jeremiah 1:7).
Prophecy is presented as God's continuing provision for his people's guidance, grounded in the pattern of Moses. The prophet's authority is derivative: he speaks because God raises him up.
A true prophet's word is borne out by events because it is God's word. The test also frees Israel from fear of those who speak presumptuously; their threats have no power the LORD has not given.

A true prophet can give his own opinion and be wrong. Nathan's authority rests not on his judgment but on the word that comes to him, and he promptly carries back a message that contradicts what he said.

The verse is the classic test case for how prophecy works. Some read it as direct prediction; others as a sign fulfilled first in Isaiah's day and fully in Christ; others as a pattern Matthew recognizes in Jesus, as he does with Hosea 11:1 in Matthew 2:15. All three readings agree that the promise of God's presence with David's house outruns any child born in Ahaz's reign.

Daniel neither broadcasts nor dismisses the vision; he keeps it. The book presents prophecy as something to be guarded and pondered until its time (12:4, 9), and the New Testament's picture of Mary pondering the words about her son stands in the same tradition of patient reception.
Jesus assumes that prophecy will continue among his people and that it must be tested. The warning is not against prophecy but against those who use it as a disguise.
Mark presents the gospel as the fulfillment of what the prophets promised. The story begins in Scripture before it begins in the Jordan valley.
John's appearance declares that prophecy, silent for generations, has returned, and specifically the Elijah Malachi promised. Jesus later confirms that Elijah has come (9:13).

The Law and the Prophets appear in their greatest figures and speak with Jesus. Luke specifies the subject, his departure (exodos) to be fulfilled in Jerusalem (Luke 9:31); Mark leaves it unstated, but in context the cross just predicted in 8:31 is the natural topic.

Jesus reads Scripture as fulfilled in unexpected forms: the promised Elijah came as a prophet in camel's hair who was executed by a petty king. The same pattern of fulfillment through rejection will hold for the Son of Man.

Whether Jesus had arranged the colt in advance or knew of it by prophetic insight, Mark tells the scene so that his word is fulfilled exactly, as Samuel's signs to Saul were fulfilled in order (1 Samuel 10:2-7). The reader learns that what Jesus says about the days ahead, including his death and rising, will come true in the same way.
The disciples ask for a timetable and signs, and Jesus answers mainly with warnings. The chapter treats prophecy as preparation for faithful living, not as a code for calculating dates.
Jesus reads Daniel as still speaking. A prophecy fulfilled once under Antiochus IV could find a further fulfillment, a pattern of repeated fulfillment common in the New Testament's use of the Old.
The prediction of the temple's fall within a generation came true in AD 70. Whatever else the verse means, that fulfillment was one reason the early church trusted Jesus' words about what remained.

The angel identifies John with the Elijah promised in Malachi. Jesus later confirms it (Luke 7:27, Matthew 11:14), though John himself denies being Elijah in person (John 1:21); the angel's phrase ‘in the spirit and power of Elijah’ explains how both are true.
After centuries in which no recognized prophet had arisen, a prophet is named at his circumcision. John will be the last prophet before the fulfillment (Luke 16:16).
‘Today’ is fulfillment language. Luke uses sēmeron at turning points (2:11, 19:9, 23:43): the promised future has arrived in the person of Jesus, and his hearers are its witnesses.

The resurrection is presented as the fulfillment of Jesus' own words as well as the Scriptures'. Luke's pattern is that God's plan is announced, then carried out, then remembered and understood, and the women are the first to move from the second step to the third.

‘Must be fulfilled’ covers promises, patterns, and prayers, not predictions only. The Psalms, which are mostly prayers, are fulfilled when the Messiah prays them and lives them out, which is a fuller sense of fulfillment than prediction and outcome.

The things to come have been read as the events of the passion and resurrection about to unfold, as the church's future and the end of history (Revelation has been cited as an example), or as the whole new order that Jesus' going inaugurates. The verse does not specify, and each reading has able defenders; what it makes clear is that the Spirit's foresight serves the same revelation.

Like Caiaphas in 11:49-52, Pilate says more than he knows. Neither the priests' protest nor Pilate's contempt can alter what the notice proclaims, and John treats the unchangeable writing as a kind of unwitting testimony that stands over the cross.

John sees even the soldiers' gambling as the fulfillment of Scripture. The psalm of the righteous sufferer is not merely illustrated but enacted in its details, and the one who prays its opening cry in the other Gospels is shown to be the one of whom it spoke.

Jesus acts to complete Scripture with full knowledge. John presents the psalms of the suffering righteous one as finding their completion in Jesus' last hour, not by coincidence but because he is the one of whom they speak.

John sees two strands of Scripture converge in one moment: the Passover lamb whose bones must remain whole, and the pierced one whom Jerusalem will look on with repentance. The soldiers act for their own reasons, and both Scriptures are fulfilled.
The gospel is presented as promise kept. Paul reads the prophets as speaking ahead of time of God's Son, which is how the apostles consistently read Israel's Scriptures (Luke 24:27, Acts 26:22-23).
